title: Dedicated eval - FP8/INT8 perf deep dive + GPU roadmap
next_steps: Redwood to share a short benchmark summary (FP8 vs INT8 vs FP16, TTFT/TPOT + throughput) for 2-3 representative models on H100/A100, with notes on methodology.
Customer to provide their prompt length distribution (p50/p95 input and output tokens) and concurrency targets for two key endpoints (chat + batch summarization).
Schedule a follow-up to review Redwood Dedicated architecture options (single-tenant pool sizing, burst policy, and regional redundancy).
If benchmarks look good, NorthBridge to start a 2-week Dedicated pilot with a pinned runtime version and agreed regression thresholds.
action_items: Mateo Alvarez - Send benchmark summary deck + one-page methodology notes to NorthBridge (Dana/Ravi) - due 2025-09-22

Allison Grant - Confirm which perf tags/metrics can be shared externally (TTFT/TPOT, tokens/sec, GPU clocks) and redact internal cluster IDs - due 2025-09-23
Dana Liu (NorthBridge) - Share 7-day histogram for input/output tokens and target p95 latency SLOs for streaming chat - due 2025-09-20

transcript:
NorthBridge Financial x Redwood Inference (Fireflies Transcript)

Recorded: 2025-09-18 17:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive (Dedicated eval)

Attendees
- Mateo Alvarez (Redwood Inference)
- Noah Patel (Redwood Inference)
- Grace Kim (Redwood Inference)
- Allison Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Dana Liu (NorthBridge Financial)
- Ravi Menon (NorthBridge Financial)
- Priya Nair (NorthBridge Financial)
- Evan Brooks (NorthBridge Financial)

Auto Summary (generated)
- NorthBridge asked for concrete FP8/INT8 performance expectations on H100 and A100 for chat-style workloads, especially TTFT and tail latency under mixed prompt sizes.
- Redwood walked through how quantized paths behave (prefill vs decode), what the runtime is doing (kernel auto-selection, batching/scheduler), and how Redwood benchmarks to avoid misleading results.
- Discussed GPU roadmap (A100 today, H100 current, H200 planned) and how Dedicated pools can be provisioned/expanded; also touched on L40S for cost-focused tiers.
- Converged on next steps: Redwood to share an external-facing benchmark summary + methodology notes; NorthBridge to share traffic shape and SLO targets to map to a right-sized Dedicated pilot.

Topics
1) What FP8 vs INT8 buys you (and where it doesn’t)
2) Prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy workloads
3) TTFT/TPOT definitions and measurement gotchas
4) Kernel selection, shape sensitivity, and long-context behavior
5) Dedicated capacity planning + GPU roadmap
6) External benchmark packet + pilot plan

Questions (captured)
- Can you commit to a p95 TTFT target for streaming chat on H100 with FP8?
- What’s your fallback behavior if FP8/INT8 hits a correctness drift threshold?
- How stable are the kernel perf numbers week-to-week (driver/CUDA changes, clocks, contention)?
- Do you support H200 and when? Any guidance on L40S for cost tiers?

---

[00:00] Mateo Alvarez: Cool, let’s get started. Thanks everyone for making the time. I’m Mateo, I run parts of the runtime side here. Noah’s our performance architect, Grace is on the FP8/INT8 kernel work, and Allison owns observability/dashboards.

[00:14] Dana Liu: Great. I’m Dana, I lead ML platform at NorthBridge. Ravi is our… basically model serving lead. Priya is infra architect. Evan is here mostly to understand timeline and commercials but he’ll probably be quiet.

[00:29] Mateo Alvarez: Sounds good. The goal today, as I understood, is: you’re evaluating Dedicated, and you want to go deeper than the marketing numbers—like what does FP8 actually do for you in a production-ish traffic shape, and what are the measurement pitfalls. And also what’s our GPU roadmap.

[00:46] Dana Liu: Yeah. We’ve been burned by benchmark decks before.

[00:49] (crosstalk)

[00:51] Ravi Menon: Specifically, we care about streaming chat. So TTFT and then token pacing. And we’re experimenting with INT8 on our side with… I guess a vLLM fork. But it’s very sensitive and sometimes it regresses on longer prompts.

[01:07] Noah Patel: Yep, that maps to what we see: prefill and decode behave very differently under quant. We can go through that. Quick check: which model families are you primarily on? Llama-ish, Qwen-ish, Mistral-ish?

[01:19] Ravi Menon: Llama and Qwen mostly. We have a 70B-ish in one product line and then a smaller 8B-ish.

[01:26] Dana Liu: And context lengths can go long. Like 8k common, 16k not rare.

[01:32] Grace Kim: Okay, long-context prefill is the spicy part for FP8, honestly.

[01:36] Mateo Alvarez: Grace will keep us honest there.

[01:39] Priya Nair: Before we go deep—Dedicated for us means single tenant GPUs, right? Not shared with other customers?

[01:45] Mateo Alvarez: Correct. Dedicated is reserved capacity. Single-tenant GPU pool. You can do one region or multi-region. We can set autoscaling policies within your pool, plus burst if you want an overflow tier, but we can talk about that later.

[02:01] Dana Liu: OK. Let’s start with performance. If we flip FP8 on, what happens to TTFT and throughput?

[02:07] Noah Patel: Let’s separate two things: (1) microbenchmarks—kernel-level GEMM/attention speed. (2) end-to-end serving—scheduler, batching, KV cache, streaming, network, etc. FP8 usually gives you meaningful throughput improvements when you’re compute-bound. But TTFT can be dominated by prefill and also queueing, so you can see cases where FP8 improves raw compute but tail gets worse if batching/scheduling isn’t tuned.

[02:32] Ravi Menon: That’s exactly what we saw. INT8 got us “tokens per second” up but p95 got worse.

[02:37] Grace Kim: Yep. There are a couple reasons. One is kernel auto-selection might choose a “fast” kernel for a shape that’s actually bad for your long prefill. Another is conversion overhead or scale/zero-point stuff in the decode loop. Another is scheduler interleaving—prefill jobs can starve decode or vice versa.

[02:55] Dana Liu: When you say FP8, what format? e4m3? e5m2? I’m not an expert but I’ve heard there’s tradeoffs.

[03:03] Grace Kim: Good question. In practice, we support e4m3 and e5m2 depending on layer and profile, but the big thing is accumulation type. We generally accumulate in FP16 (or BF16) to keep drift bounded. The exact choice can be profile-dependent by model family.

[03:19] Ravi Menon: And INT8—are you doing per-channel? per-tensor? is it like smooth quant?

[03:24] Grace Kim: Mostly per-channel weights, and activation quantization depends on the path. We have quantization profiles that define what ops are quantized and what falls back. We’re very conservative with certain layers that are known to be accuracy sensitive.

[03:40] Dana Liu: So, in Dedicated, can we choose FP8 vs INT8 per model?

[03:45] Mateo Alvarez: Yes. You can pin the model version and the quant profile. Also we can set policy for fallback—like if drift checks fail or the kernel path is unstable, it can fall back to FP16 variant. That’s usually behind a runtime flag and an allowlist.

[04:01] Priya Nair: How do you detect drift? Are you like comparing logits? Or outputs?

[04:05] Noah Patel: We do a couple levels. In CI we run numeric drift checks against an FP16 baseline on a small prompt set—think compare token probabilities within tolerance, and then some “does the output change drastically” heuristics. For production, we don’t do full baselines obviously, but we can do canarying and alert on quality regressions via eval harnesses.

[04:26] Dana Liu: Okay. But practically—what numbers should we expect? Like if we have H100s, streaming chat, 8k prompt, 300 tokens output.

[04:35] Noah Patel: We’ll give you a benchmark summary after this. But I want to set expectation: TTFT is heavily impacted by prefill compute and queueing. FP8 generally improves the prefill compute component, but if you’re already queueing or you’re bandwidth-bound, the gain is smaller. The best case we see is: FP8 reduces cost-per-token and increases sustainable throughput at a given latency target.

[04:57] Ravi Menon: So you’re not going to promise “2x faster” on TTFT.

[05:00] Mateo Alvarez: Not without your workload details. But we can be concrete once we match your traffic shape.

[05:06] Dana Liu: That’s fair.

[05:08] Allison Grant: Also, TTFT measurement itself can be misleading. Some folks measure server-side start-of-request to first token emitted; some measure client-received; streaming chunk sizes matter; and if you have warmup not done, your first run looks terrible.

[05:23] Ravi Menon: Yep. We saw like a 2x swing depending on whether the GPU clocks are pinned.

[05:28] Grace Kim: Exactly. If you don’t pin clocks or at least control power states, you’ll benchmark “GPU wakeup.”

[05:33] Dana Liu: Can you explain your methodology? Like how do you benchmark so we can trust it.

[05:38] Noah Patel: Sure. The short version:
- Environment pinning: same container digest, pinned runtime commit, driver/CUDA version documented.
- Warmup: run enough requests to populate KV cache paths and compilation caches (if any) before measuring.
- Repetitions: multiple runs per point, report median and p95/p99, and we do outlier rejection when a node is contended.
- Fixed traffic shape: we define prompt length distributions, concurrency, and streaming parameters; not just a single prompt.
- Phase timing: we split into prefill and decode, and report TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per output token) separately.

[06:24] Priya Nair: You said “outlier rejection”—that makes me nervous. Like you just drop bad runs?

[06:29] Noah Patel: Good callout. We only drop runs that fail health checks (e.g., another job stole the GPU, clocks were not set, obvious telemetry gaps). Otherwise, we include variance. In the report we can show both the raw distribution and the filtered summary.

[06:46] Dana Liu: And what about continuous batching? Because that changes everything.

[06:50] Noah Patel: We run with the production scheduler on. For microbenchmarks, we isolate kernels. For end-to-end, we use realistic concurrency and let the scheduler batch.

[07:01] Ravi Menon: How do you handle mixed prompt lengths? That’s our reality. Some prompts are like 200 tokens, some are 12k.

[07:08] Grace Kim: Mixed lengths are where scheduler policy matters. If you let huge prefill requests batch with tiny ones, the small ones can get dragged. Our newer policy tries to cap batch sizes for decode and control interleaving.

[07:21] Dana Liu: Is that in the product now or experimental?

[07:24] Mateo Alvarez: It’s behind knobs today. We typically roll it out via canary. For Dedicated, we can set those knobs per pool if needed.

[07:33] Priya Nair: Dedicated means we can tune scheduler settings without affecting other customers?

[07:37] Mateo Alvarez: Yep. That’s one of the benefits.

[07:41] Evan Brooks: Sorry, quick question—does that change pricing? Like if we change knobs and throughput changes.

[07:46] Mateo Alvarez: Dedicated is a capacity contract, so it’s not per-token. We size the pool based on your throughput and latency requirements. If we can make it more efficient, that’s good for you and for us.

[07:58] Dana Liu: Back to GPU roadmap. We’re hearing H200 is better for memory bandwidth and context. Are you supporting it?

[08:05] Mateo Alvarez: We’re actively bringing H200 into our perf lab and then into Dedicated regions. Today, H100 and A100 are widely available, with some L40S options. H200 availability depends on region and quotas, but we can plan for it in Q4/Q1.

[08:22] Ravi Menon: Do you have numbers showing H200 vs H100 for long context? Like 16k prefill.

[08:28] Noah Patel: We have early internal numbers but we need to be careful because it depends on kernel tuning and driver stack. H200 tends to help in memory-heavy regimes. For long context, attention and KV cache traffic can become bandwidth bound, so H200’s memory can help. But again, the headline isn’t just “H200 fixes it”—scheduler and kernel selection still matter.

[08:53] Grace Kim: Also FP8 on H200 may not be automatically “best” unless the kernel tuning table is updated. We’ve seen tile config differences matter.

[09:01] Dana Liu: So the thing we care about is: we don’t want to sign a Dedicated contract and then find out FP8 is unstable and we have to run FP16.

[09:09] Mateo Alvarez: Totally fair. That’s why we propose a pilot with pinned runtime version and explicit guardrails: you get a stable baseline; we can test FP8/INT8 on your prompts; if quality or tail latency is off, we can fall back to FP16 for the sensitive endpoints.

[09:25] Allison Grant: And we can expose per-endpoint metrics: TTFT p50/p95, TPOT, queue wait time, and tagging by quant mode. So you can see “is FP8 actually helping or is it just causing queueing.”

[09:39] Priya Nair: Are those metrics available in our systems? Like export to Datadog? Or only your console.

[09:44] Allison Grant: For Dedicated, we can do both: console dashboards and export via supported sinks. We can also provide audit logs and request tracing if needed.

[09:55] Dana Liu: OK. Ravi, do you want to ask the kernel-level questions.

[09:58] Ravi Menon: Yeah. On INT8, we’ve seen overhead on conversion and sometimes dequant happens inside the matmul path. Are you fusing that? Or is it separate kernels.

[10:09] Grace Kim: We try to fuse where it’s safe. There are cases where conversion overhead dominates for small batch decode. We’ve been reducing that by fusing dequant and avoiding redundant scale conversions in the decode loop.

[10:24] Ravi Menon: And kernel selection. How do you choose kernels? Is it heuristic based on shape, or autotuning.

[10:30] Grace Kim: It’s heuristic + capability detection. It looks at shape, dtype, device, sequence lengths, and selects among a set of optimized kernels. We also log the chosen kernel family and shapes when the tracing flag is enabled.

[10:47] Dana Liu: That logging—does it add overhead?

[10:49] Grace Kim: Minimal, but we keep it guarded behind a flag. For benchmarking, we turn it on to attribute performance. For production, we typically keep it off unless debugging.

[11:03] Noah Patel: One thing to watch: if kernel selection picks an FP16 kernel accidentally for an INT8 shape, you’ll get perf cliff. We have checks to prevent that, but it’s a class of bug that happens.

[11:17] Ravi Menon: We had that exact thing.

[11:18] Dana Liu: Great…

[11:19] (laughter)

[11:22] Priya Nair: For Dedicated, are you running on bare metal or VMs? And do we get control on driver versions?

[11:29] Mateo Alvarez: Generally VMs with dedicated GPUs, depending on region. Driver stack is pinned by us, but for Dedicated we can coordinate upgrades and keep you on a stable train. We usually don’t let customers arbitrarily pick driver versions, but we can hold or advance with notice.

[11:47] Dana Liu: So how do you ensure reproducible benchmarks if the environment changes.

[11:52] Noah Patel: That’s why we pin containers and runtime commits, and we track driver/CUDA versions as metadata. When something changes, we re-baseline and set regression thresholds.

[12:05] Ravi Menon: What are your regression thresholds? Like what’s considered a “stop ship.”

[12:10] Mateo Alvarez: We define thresholds per metric. For quantized paths, we’re stricter on correctness and tail latency. Example: if p95 TTFT regresses beyond an agreed percent for the standard workload, it fails canary. If it’s a small throughput regression but correctness is fine, we might allow it with mitigation.

[12:31] Dana Liu: For us, TTFT p95 is the headline. We can tolerate throughput being slightly lower if TTFT is stable.

[12:38] Noah Patel: Good. That aligns with how we typically optimize streaming experiences.

[12:44] ---

[12:45] (screen share referenced) Noah Patel: I’m going to share a conceptual chart. This is not your exact numbers, but it shows decomposition. Prefill time scales roughly with input tokens; decode time scales with output tokens. FP8 helps both but often more on the compute-heavy part. However, if the scheduler batches too aggressively, TTFT can worsen because you’re waiting to form a batch.

[13:10] Dana Liu: So you would cap batch size to protect TTFT.

[13:13] Noah Patel: Exactly. Especially for decode. And for prefill, we may separate “long prefill lane” from short ones.

[13:22] Priya Nair: Like two queues.

[13:24] Noah Patel: Conceptually, yes. We do it via policy and backpressure.

[13:30] Ravi Menon: Is there a risk that FP8 makes prefill faster but then decode becomes the bottleneck and you still don’t win.

[13:36] Grace Kim: Yes. That’s why you need both FP8 kernels and KV cache/decoder loop optimizations. And sometimes INT8 wins on decode but FP8 wins on prefill. It’s not one-size.

[13:51] Dana Liu: Wait, that’s interesting. So we might want FP8 for long-context prefill heavy endpoints, and INT8 for decode heavy?

[13:58] Grace Kim: Potentially. Or mixed. But operationally it’s easier to pick one per model variant. We can evaluate both on your workload.

[14:10] Allison Grant: And we can show phase breakdowns so it’s not a black box.

[14:14] Dana Liu: OK.

[14:16] ---

[14:17] Ravi Menon: Can you talk about long-context regressions? We saw something like alignment issues, where 16k prompt causes weird slowdowns.

[14:24] Grace Kim: Yeah, there are a few known pitfalls. Sometimes attention kernels have assumptions about block alignment. If your sequence length hits an unlucky boundary, you can see performance drop or even correctness issues. We’ve been patching those cases. For benchmarking, we include boundary lengths, not just round numbers.

[14:44] Dana Liu: Do you test 8192, 8193 type things.

[14:48] Grace Kim: Exactly. And 16384, 16385. Those catch alignment bugs.

[14:54] Noah Patel: Also, watch out for “first token” being slow if KV cache isn’t allocated or memory pools aren’t warmed.

[15:03] Dana Liu: OK. Switching gears. Dedicated sizing: we have two workloads. One is real-time chat, spiky. Another is batch summarization overnight. Can we share the pool.

[15:14] Mateo Alvarez: Yes, but we should be careful: mixing batch with latency-sensitive traffic can harm tail latency. We can do time-based scheduling—run batch at night—or use separate pools or priority lanes.

[15:28] Priya Nair: We’d prefer one pool for budget reasons.

[15:32] Mateo Alvarez: Understood. We can start with one pool and enforce priority and caps. But we’ll need your peak concurrency and SLO.

[15:41] Dana Liu: Our peak is… not sure we want to say on the call.

[15:44] Mateo Alvarez: You can send it offline.

[15:47] Evan Brooks: We’ll share ranges.

[15:50] ---

[15:51] Ravi Menon: Competitors: we’re also looking at AWS’s managed endpoints and Together. Together is pushing FP8 heavily.

[15:59] Mateo Alvarez: Makes sense. The core thing we’d emphasize is: Dedicated gives you isolation and predictable scheduling. Hosted APIs can be great, but if you want consistent p95 under your exact traffic, Dedicated helps. And we’ll show you the benchmark methodology so it’s apples-to-apples.

[16:17] Dana Liu: For compliance, we likely need audit logs and data retention controls. But that might be a separate call.

[16:24] Mateo Alvarez: Yep, we can loop in security. For today we’ll stay performance.

[16:29] ---

[16:30] Allison Grant: Quick note on what we can share externally. We can share TTFT/TPOT and tokens/sec, and the environment details at a high level (GPU SKU, driver major version, runtime build). We won’t share internal cluster hostnames, but you’ll get enough to reproduce in a pilot.

[16:48] Dana Liu: That’s fine.

[16:50] Priya Nair: One more infra question: do you support multi-region active/active in Dedicated.

[16:56] Mateo Alvarez: We support multi-region pools. Active/active at the app level, yes. The control plane supports routing policies. For the pilot, we usually do one region to keep variables down.

[17:10] Dana Liu: OK.

[17:12] ---

[17:13] (timestamp drift - transcription)

[17:14] Noah Patel: Let’s talk about how we’ll structure the benchmark packet you want. We’ll do:
1) Two or three representative models (one ~8B, one ~70B class, depending on what we can share)
2) H100 + A100 results. If we have H200 by then, we’ll add a “preview” with caveats.
3) Three workloads: prefill-heavy long context, decode-heavy short prompt, and mixed distribution streaming chat.
4) Report TTFT p50/p95, TPOT p50/p95, throughput tokens/sec, and cost proxy.

[17:54] Dana Liu: Cost proxy?

[17:56] Noah Patel: Basically, tokens per GPU-second. It’s not your exact dollar number, but it helps compare.

[18:04] Ravi Menon: Will you include confidence intervals?

[18:06] Noah Patel: We’ll include run-to-run variance and number of repetitions. We can also show a box plot style summary.

[18:15] Dana Liu: Great.

[18:17] ---

[18:18] Grace Kim: One nuance: INT8 sometimes looks great on decode but can have correctness sensitivities depending on the model. We’ll annotate where we had to fall back certain layers.

[18:31] Dana Liu: That’s important. We need something we can put in front of our internal model governance group.

[18:37] Priya Nair: And our risk team will ask “how do you ensure outputs are not wildly different.”

[18:43] Mateo Alvarez: We’ll include a short section on guardrails and rollout: canarying, drift checks, and fallback policies.

[18:52] Ravi Menon: In our experience, drift is not just “wrong answer,” it’s like subtle. Hallucinations can increase.

[18:58] Grace Kim: Yep. Quant can change logit margins and sampling. So we typically run with deterministic decoding for evals (temperature 0) and then sanity check with a few stochastic runs.

[19:12] Dana Liu: OK.

[19:14] ---

[19:15] (mid-call deeper kernel discussion)

[19:16] Ravi Menon: For FP8, do you do per-layer scaling. Or is it global.

[19:20] Grace Kim: Per-layer, and sometimes per-channel. Again, depends on profile. The scaling strategy is part of the quant profile. For inference, we keep it stable; we’re not doing dynamic calibration per request.

[19:36] Ravi Menon: And if shapes change—like variable batch sizes—does the kernel retune.

[19:41] Grace Kim: No dynamic autotune in the hot path. We rely on pre-tuned kernels. Shape changes can affect which kernel is chosen.

[19:50] Noah Patel: That’s why logging the chosen kernel and shape is so useful when you see weird perf cliffs.

[19:58] Dana Liu: Would we get that logging in our Dedicated pilot?

[20:01] Mateo Alvarez: Yes, in a debug mode. We’ll coordinate to keep overhead low.

[20:06] Allison Grant: And we can sample it. Not 100% of requests.

[20:10] Dana Liu: Great.

[20:12] ---

[20:13] Priya Nair: What about MIG? Do you use MIG on H100?

[20:17] Mateo Alvarez: In general, Dedicated pools are full GPUs unless there’s a specific reason. MIG can help with isolation for small workloads, but for LLM serving it can complicate scheduling and reduce peak efficiency depending on partition. We can discuss if you want smaller slices for dev/test.

[20:36] Dana Liu: We probably want full GPUs.

[20:39] ---

[20:40] Evan Brooks: On timeline: if we like the benchmark packet, how quickly can we start a pilot.

[20:46] Mateo Alvarez: Usually within 1-3 weeks depending on region and GPU availability. H100 is generally fastest. A100 also. H200 is tighter.

[20:57] Evan Brooks: OK.

[21:00] Dana Liu: We want this in Q4.

[21:03] Mateo Alvarez: That’s feasible.

[21:05] ---

[21:06] (discussion around streaming definitions)

[21:07] Ravi Menon: Let’s align definitions. TTFT for us is: from request accepted to first token received by client.

[21:14] Noah Patel: We can measure both server-side and client-side. In our harness we usually report server-side TTFT and include a note. For the pilot we can instrument client-perceived too.

[21:28] Dana Liu: And TPOT?

[21:30] Noah Patel: Time per output token, often measured as (time between tokens) averaged over the decode. We also report p95 per-token time because streaming jitter matters.

[21:44] Allison Grant: Some people call it “token cadence.” We can give you both.

[21:49] Dana Liu: Perfect.

[21:52] ---

[21:53] (minor transcription error)

[21:54] Speaker 1: So for the benchmarks, do you fix temperature.

[21:57] Grace Kim: For perf, yes. We fix decoding params: temperature, top-p, max tokens, stop sequences. For quality sanity, we test a couple settings.

[22:08] Ravi Menon: We have function calling and JSON schema sometimes.

[22:12] Mateo Alvarez: For now we’ll benchmark the underlying generation. But we can add a structured output scenario in the pilot if it affects token patterns.

[22:22] Dana Liu: Function calling increases tool latency, but that’s outside model.

[22:26] Noah Patel: Right.

[22:28] ---

[22:29] (tail latency & queueing)

[22:30] Priya Nair: A big concern is multi-tenant noise. We have experienced noisy neighbors in cloud. Dedicated helps, but what about internal contention in your cluster.

[22:41] Mateo Alvarez: Dedicated pools are isolated from other customers. Internally we still have host-level processes, but we avoid colocating unrelated jobs. Also, for benchmarking we use isolated nodes.

[22:55] Noah Patel: In our canary and perf lab, we enforce no background jobs and pinned clocks. In production Dedicated, we can apply similar isolation policies.

[23:06] Dana Liu: OK.

[23:08] ---

[23:09] (GPU roadmap details)

[23:10] Mateo Alvarez: On roadmap: near-term we’re expanding H100 capacity in the main regions. H200 comes as we secure supply; we’ll likely start with a limited set of regions and expand. L40S is an option for cost-sensitive smaller models.

[23:29] Ravi Menon: Would you ever recommend L40S for 70B.

[23:32] Noah Patel: Generally no, not for latency-sensitive 70B. Maybe for batch. But we can talk about it.

[23:40] Dana Liu: We prefer fewer SKUs to manage.

[23:43] Mateo Alvarez: That’s typical. Many customers standardize on H100.

[23:48] ---

[23:49] (more kernel notes)

[23:50] Ravi Menon: One more: we saw INT8 regress on specific shapes. Like batch=7, seq=2049.

[23:57] Grace Kim: That sounds like a kernel selection edge case. It might pick a fallback kernel. That’s exactly why we log the chosen kernel plus shapes. In our benchmark packet, we can also include notes about shape sensitivity.

[24:16] Dana Liu: Okay.

[24:18] ---

[24:19] (Pilot discussion)

[24:20] Mateo Alvarez: So, pilot proposal: we start with one model endpoint, one region, H100 pool sized for your peak p95 target. We run FP16 baseline first to validate infrastructure, then we test FP8 and INT8 profiles. We decide on a default, with fallback policy.

[24:43] Dana Liu: We’d need to include our own eval prompts.

[24:46] Mateo Alvarez: Yes.

[24:47] Priya Nair: And security review will run in parallel.

[24:50] Mateo Alvarez: Yep.

[24:52] ---

[24:53] (wrap-up begins)

[24:54] Dana Liu: This was helpful. The key thing is the external benchmark packet. Our CTO will want something tangible.

[25:01] Mateo Alvarez: Understood. We’ll send a short summary deck plus a one-pager on methodology. We’ll keep it defensible and include caveats.

[25:12] Ravi Menon: Please include TTFT and TPOT, and ideally separate prefill/decode.

[25:16] Noah Patel: Will do.

[25:18] Dana Liu: And maybe mention what you did about GPU clocks / warmup so it doesn’t look like magic.

[25:23] Allison Grant: Yep, we’ll note that.

[25:26] Evan Brooks: And then we’ll schedule follow up next week?

[25:29] Mateo Alvarez: Yes. Talia from our side (program manager) will coordinate scheduling—though she’s not on today.

[25:36] Dana Liu: Great.

[25:38] ---

[25:39] (final recap)

[25:40] Mateo Alvarez: Recap:
1) You’ll send us prompt/token distributions and SLO targets.
2) We’ll send benchmark summary + methodology notes early next week.
3) We’ll schedule a follow-up to review Dedicated sizing and pilot plan.
4) If that looks good, we kick off a 2-week pilot with pinned versions and explicit regression thresholds.

[26:05] Dana Liu: Sounds good.

[26:07] Ravi Menon: Thanks.

[26:08] Priya Nair: Thank you.

[26:10] Mateo Alvarez: Thanks all.

(Transcript ends — remaining time was small talk / scheduling; not fully captured.)
